Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Vignette:
The event that had reshaped Leo’s life happened three years ago, during a fishing season that had started like any other. He was twenty-three, a deckhand on a commercial trawler out of Gloucester, when the boat was boarded off the coast by a paramilitary group that had been extorting the fleet. They had taken him and two others below deck, bound them to metal pipes in the hold, and spent the next six hours beating them with batons and burning them with cigarette ends while demanding the location of a rival captain. Leo had been stripped to his underwear, his wrists tied behind his back to a cold pipe, his knees pressed into the damp steel floor. Every time he tried to shift his weight, the rope cut deeper. He could hear the baby of the boat’s cook crying from the cabin above—a high, thin wail that cut through the shouting. That sound had stayed with him, lodged like a fishhook in his memory.

In the months that followed, Leo had tried to return to work, but the boat was no longer a place of competence and routine. When the engine hummed at a certain frequency, his body would lock into the exact posture of that night: shoulders forward, wrists twisted behind his back, knees pressed into a hard surface. It happened without warning—a flicker of engine vibration, and suddenly he was back in the hold, the pain in his wrists and knees surging as if the ropes were still there. He would feel the old burn marks on his ribs throb, even though the wounds had healed years ago. The rage that came with these memories was overwhelming—a hot, shaking fury that left him gripping the railing until his knuckles went white, wanting to smash something, someone.

He left fishing and took a job driving a delivery truck, but that brought its own problems. The first time he rode a bus to the licensing office, a baby started crying in the seat behind him, and Leo had to get off at the next stop, his heart hammering, his palms slick. He came to believe that the sound of a crying baby was a direct signal that something terrible was about to happen. He started avoiding public transport entirely, walking miles instead, even in winter rain. At home, he rearranged the furniture so that every chair and sofa faced the door, with his back to a solid wall. He could not sit in a restaurant or a waiting room unless he had a corner seat. His wife, Maria, found him one night standing in the dark of their living room, listening. When she asked what he was doing, he said he was checking if anyone was trying to get in through the back window. He had begun, without quite deciding to, to scan every room for objects that could be used as weapons—a fire extinguisher, a heavy lamp, a kitchen knife left on the counter. He catalogued them automatically, noting their location and weight, as if he might need to grab one in an instant.

The worst was the feeling of emotional vulnerability. If Maria raised her voice in an argument, even about something trivial like a forgotten grocery item, Leo’s body would go cold and rigid. He had come to interpret any expression of anger or disappointment from her as the first step toward something violent. He stopped disagreeing with her, stopped bringing up his own needs, because the feeling of being emotionally exposed had become indistinguishable from the feeling of being tied to that pipe. Over the months, he pulled away from her, spending more time in the garage or walking alone along the docks at night, watching the boats he no longer trusted.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment on the delivery route last week. He had stopped at a red light, and a woman with a stroller crossed in front of his truck. The baby in the stroller began to cry. Leo’s wrists went numb. He felt the rope again, the cold metal, the burning on his ribs. His vision narrowed, and when the light turned green he could not move his foot to the gas pedal. He sat there through two full cycles of the traffic light, shaking, until the driver behind him laid on the horn. That sound—sharp, insistent—sent a bolt of rage through him so intense he nearly put his fist through the dashboard. He pulled over and called his wife, his voice breaking, and told her he needed help. He is terrified that the next time the rage comes, he will hurt someone. He is equally terrified that the next time the fear comes, he will simply stop being able to move at all.
